title: Voice Memo to a Daughter I Haven't Met Yet
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Recording this at midnight, hours before surgery, because there are things I want you to inherit besides my stubborn chin and my regrettable singing voice.
Narrator: The doctors keep using the word routine, a word doing a great deal of unpaid labor tonight.
Narrator: [carefully] I am not afraid of dying, not exactly. I am afraid of dying before telling you what I actually believe, as opposed to what I performed believing at dinner parties.
Narrator: Here is the inheritance: everything that happens to me tonight, the good outcome and the other one, arrives from the same hand, however unevenly I've managed to accept that symmetry.
Narrator: [reflective] I spent my twenties treating tawakkul as a consolation prize, something reached for only once competence had visibly failed you.
Narrator: It took considerably longer than it should have to notice that competence was never mine to claim outright, only ever borrowed, on terms I didn't set myself.
Narrator: [honestly] If you're hearing this because the other outcome arrived, know I didn't surrender to it. I simply stopped mistaking surrender for despair somewhere along the way.
Narrator: There's a difference, one your grandmother tried explaining for years before I finally stopped arguing long enough to actually listen to her.
Narrator: [gently] Despair insists the story has ended. What I feel tonight is closer to handing the pen back to its actual author, mid-sentence, without demanding to see the ending first.
Narrator: I won't pretend this is serene. My hands are shaking slightly, and serenity was never really the promise anyway.
Narrator: [calmly] The promise, as I understand it, was never comfort. It was company, of a kind no corridor can fully replace, however earnestly it tries.
Narrator: So, whoever you become, question everything else I taught you, but not this: certainty was never the actual point. Steadiness, even trembling steadiness, was always the real assignment.
Narrator: [encouraging] I love you already, extravagantly, on the strength of nothing but potential, which strikes me tonight as an oddly accurate description of faith itself.
Narrator: They're calling my name now. Alhamdulillah, for tonight and whatever tomorrow decides to become. I'll finish this properly, one way or another, my love.

title: A Late Podcast on Whether Predestination Cancels the Game
script: Host: [thoughtful] Insomniac listeners, tonight's question arrived from a chess player, of all people, who wants to know whether qadar renders the entire match a formality.
Guest: A wonderfully specific anxiety. I take it he means: if the outcome is already authored, why bother studying openings at all.
Host: [carefully] Precisely his objection. Why deliberate, if the deliberation was never going to alter anything in the first place.
Guest: The trouble is it smuggles in a spectator's vantage point and hands it to the player, who has no access to it whatsoever.
Host: [reflective] Isn't that simply changing the subject rather than answering it, Professor.
Guest: Fair accusation. Let me answer properly, then. The player's ignorance of the outcome isn't a flaw, it's the entire condition under which choice retains meaning for him.
Host: [honestly] So foreknowledge on Allah's part doesn't collapse the player's agency, because the player was never operating from that vantage to begin with.
Guest: Exactly right. Authorship and agency occupy different registers entirely, and conflating them produces precisely this kind of vertigo among otherwise careful thinkers.
Host: [gently] Doesn't that feel like a technicality dressed up as comfort, though, to someone genuinely unsettled tonight.
Guest: It would be, if I were offering it as comfort. I'm offering it as clarification. Comfort, if it arrives, comes from somewhere else entirely.
Host: [calmly] Where, then.
Guest: In realizing the game was never a solitary performance graded from a distance. It was always played in the company of the one who authored the board itself.
Host: [encouraging] That's a considerably more generous reframing than the fairly cold doctrine usually receives from its critics.
Guest: Doctrines only read as cold in isolation. Embedded in relationship, qadar stops resembling fatalism and starts resembling something closer to accompaniment.
Host: [seriously] And for listeners who still feel the vertigo, despite tonight's chess lesson.
Guest: I'd tell them vertigo is an entirely reasonable response to standing near something considerably larger than themselves. I still feel it some nights, credentials notwithstanding.
Host: On that admirably honest note, we'll let tonight's chess player return to his opening theory.
Guest: Tell him to play boldly. The board was never counting on his hesitation anyway.

title: Two Brothers at Their Father's Bedside
script: Idris: [thoughtful] You flew in eleven hours and still haven't said a single word to him. What exactly are you waiting for, Karim.
Karim: Permission, maybe. I spent a decade convinced his heart attack was somehow a verdict on how thoroughly I'd disappointed him.
Idris: [carefully] That's absurd, and you clearly know it's absurd, even as you're saying it out loud to me.
Karim: Knowing it's absurd hasn't stopped it from governing roughly a decade of unreturned phone calls, apparently, however irrational that sounds now.
Idris: [reflective] Qadar doesn't distribute blame that precisely, Karim. His heart failing wasn't a referendum on your career choices, whatever story you've built around it.
Karim: I understand that theologically. I haven't managed to feel it yet, if I'm being entirely honest with you tonight.
Idris: [honestly] Neither have I, entirely. I've been sitting here for three days constructing my own private ledger of everything I should have done differently.
Karim: Does the ledger balance any better than mine does, after three days of practice.
Idris: [gently] Not remotely. I've simply had three more days of practice pretending it does, which isn't the same accomplishment at all.
Karim: Maybe that's the actual test tonight, not whether we can explain why this happened, but whether we can sit with him without demanding an explanation first.
Idris: [calmly] That sounds like something Mom would have said, considerably more gracefully than either of us just managed between us.
Karim: She'd have said trust doesn't require the ledger to balance. It just requires showing up while the account is still open to us.
Idris: [encouraging] Then go. The account's still open, Karim. It won't stay that way indefinitely, however much we'd both prefer otherwise.
Karim: Okay. Wish me an opening line that isn't apology dressed up as small talk, because I genuinely don't have one yet.
Idris: [seriously] Tell him you're here. Everything else can wait for tomorrow, if Allah grants us one after tonight.
Karim: Alright. Wish me steadier hands than I currently have walking into that room.
Idris: You won't need steady hands, Karim. You'll just need to walk through that door.

title: The Retired Judge's Meditation on Justice and Mercy
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Thirty-one years on the bench taught me that justice, administered by human hands, is always approximate, however carefully we dress it in procedure and precedent.
Narrator: I sentenced men I believed were guilty and later doubted, acquitted others I privately suspected weren't innocent, and carried both verdicts home nightly regardless.
Narrator: [carefully] What unsettled me most wasn't error, error is survivable enough. It was the certainty with which I'd delivered verdicts I now recognize as provisional at best.
Narrator: Tauhid, oddly enough, is what eventually steadied that unease, not by excusing my mistakes but by relocating final judgment somewhere my fallibility couldn't reach it.
Narrator: [reflective] There's a particular arrogance in believing one's own gavel is the last word on anyone's account, an arrogance the robe encourages rather more than it should.
Narrator: I used to think divine justice simply meant a stricter, more accurate version of what I practiced daily, a cosmic upgrade to my own courtroom procedures.

Narrator: [honestly] I no longer think that. Mercy, in the accounts I've studied since retiring, isn't justice's exception. It's frequently justice's actual substance, dispensed by someone who sees what evidence never fully captures.

Narrator: Motive, circumstance, the entire unrecorded interior of a person's life, all invisible to a courtroom, all apparently visible to the only judge whose ruling won't require an appeal afterward.
Narrator: [gently] That used to unsettle me, the asymmetry of it. Now I find something close to relief in a jurisdiction I was never actually qualified to preside over myself.
Narrator: My grandson asked recently whether I missed the authority. I told him I'd traded it for something considerably better, the privilege of no longer needing to be right about everyone.
Narrator: [calmly] I still read case files sometimes, out of habit more than duty, and I still notice precisely where my younger self overreached his actual jurisdiction back then.
Narrator: These days I simply note the overreach, forgive the man who made it, and trust the remaining ledger to hands considerably steadier than mine ever were.

title: A Grandfather's Story About the Merchant Who Counted Stars
script: Aisyah: [thoughtful] Kek, why do you always look at the sky before you tell a story, every single time without fail.
Grandfather: Habit, from a story my own grandfather told me, about a merchant who tried counting the stars one particularly restless night.
Aisyah: [carefully] Counting them, why would anyone count stars, there are so clearly too many to manage.
Grandfather: That was rather his point, once he'd exhausted himself past a few thousand. He'd set out to catalogue creation tidily, before sunrise arrived.
Aisyah: [reflective] That sounds like a very silly plan, Kek, honestly.
Grandfather: It was, though he didn't think so at the time. Men rarely recognize their own silliness while they're actively committing to it.
Aisyah: [honestly] What happened when the sun finally came up over him.
Grandfather: He'd counted, by his own inflated estimate, perhaps four thousand, and realized he hadn't moved past a single visible quadrant of the actual sky.
Aisyah: [gently] Did that make him sad, Kek, after all that counting.
Grandfather: Briefly, yes. Then something shifted, and the sadness became something closer to relief, oddly enough, as the sun rose fully.
Aisyah: [calmly] Relief, why would that bring him relief instead of more disappointment.
Grandfather: Because he realized he'd been carrying creation's entire ledger alone, unnecessarily, when it was never actually his to carry in the first place.
Aisyah: [encouraging] So he just stopped counting, and gave up entirely on the whole idea.
Grandfather: He stopped counting, and started simply looking instead, which apparently felt entirely different, though the stars themselves hadn't changed at all.
Aisyah: [seriously] I think I understand, Kek. It's like when I try fixing everything about my exam grades alone, and Mama says I'm not the only one holding it.
Grandfather: That's precisely it, cucu. Tauhid doesn't ask you to stop counting entirely. It asks you to remember whose ledger it actually is.
Aisyah: I like this story much better than the ones with dragons, Kek, I have to admit.
Grandfather: Give it time. This one grows on you considerably longer than any dragon story ever does.

title: Notes from an Astronomer Who Stopped Needing Answers
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] I've spent eighteen years photographing light that left its source before human beings existed to notice its eventual arrival.
Narrator: Colleagues assume that vantage breeds either atheism or a very particular kind of vertigo. Mine, apparently, bred something closer to the opposite entirely.
Narrator: [carefully] The scale doesn't diminish the question of a creator, whatever popular science writing insists confidently. It simply raises the entry price for taking the question seriously.
Narrator: I used to think faith required a smaller universe, something modest enough for a single deity to plausibly administer without any assistance whatsoever.
Narrator: [reflective] That assumption said considerably more about the limits of my own imagination than about anything resembling actual theology, in hindsight.
Narrator: Tauhid, properly understood, was never claiming a cramped cosmos. It was claiming a single, undivided authorship across whatever scale the cosmos actually turns out to occupy.

Narrator: [honestly] I find that, if anything, considerably more staggering than any competing account I've encountered, religious or otherwise, across eighteen years of looking upward professionally.
Narrator: My daughter asked recently whether all those light-years made me feel small. I told her smallness was never quite the sensation, precision was the closer word.

Narrator: [gently] A single hand steadying something this vast, this old, this indifferent to my personal timeline, requires a precision I can't casually attribute to accident, however patiently accident gets argued for.
Narrator: I don't say this to settle an argument I know remains genuinely unsettled among people considerably more credentialed than I currently am.
Narrator: [calmly] I say it because the telescope, unexpectedly, became the instrument that returned me to prayer, not the one that finally excused me from it.

Narrator: Some nights I still sit at the eyepiece long after data collection ends, for no reason the grant committee would formally accept, simply to remain a while in the presence of something evidently authored.

title: A Radio Segment on Whether Gratitude Is a Discipline or a Feeling
script: Radio Host: [thoughtful] Tonight's question comes from a listener who says gratitude feels performative whenever she forces it, and wants to know if forced gratitude actually counts at all.
Guest: A wonderfully honest question, and one shukr, properly understood, anticipated centuries before wellness culture rediscovered it as a modern trend.
Radio Host: [carefully] Anticipated it how, exactly, if you'd unpack that for us tonight.
Guest: Shukr was never framed primarily as a feeling summoned on command. It was framed as a discipline, considerably closer to a muscle than a passing mood.
Radio Host: [reflective] But doesn't disciplined gratitude risk becoming hollow, a script recited without any interior conviction actually behind it.
Guest: It risks that, certainly, the way any discipline risks hollowness before the practice matures into something felt rather than merely performed for show.
Radio Host: [honestly] So hollowness in the beginning doesn't disqualify the practice over the long term, in your view.
Guest: Not remotely. Muscles feel entirely artificial too, during the first several attempts, before the body quietly reorganizes itself around the new exercise.
Radio Host: [gently] What does that reorganization actually look like, practically, for someone starting from genuine resentment rather than simple neutrality.
Guest: It looks like naming one specific, concrete mercy daily, refusing the vague, general gratitude that costs a person nothing whatsoever to recite.
Radio Host: [calmly] Why does specificity matter quite so much in this particular discipline.
Guest: Vague gratitude flatters the speaker without implicating them in anything real. Specific gratitude requires actually noticing, which is considerably harder and considerably more honest.
Radio Host: [encouraging] And if someone notices, faithfully, for months, and still feels nothing genuinely shift internally.
Guest: Then I'd say the feeling was never the actual metric to begin with. The noticing was, and the noticing quietly changes a person regardless of whether it announces itself emotionally.
Radio Host: [seriously] That reframes the entire question rather elegantly for our anxious caller tonight, I think.
Guest: Tell her the forcing isn't dishonesty. It's simply training arriving before conviction does, which is how most disciplines, religious or otherwise, actually work.

title: Between Planning Carefully and Pretending to Control the Outcome
script: Narrator: [reflective] During a difficult job search, a friend said he could no longer tell the difference between healthy planning and the illusion that a perfect plan would guarantee a result.

Narrator: His question opened a rich discussion about tawakkul. Trust in Allah does not turn lawful effort into a superstition, nor does it make effort unnecessary. It changes the place we give effort in our hearts.
Narrator: He revised his application materials, sought feedback, checked whether roles were permissible for him, and set a realistic schedule for searching. Those were means, not promises.

Narrator: When an interview did not lead to an offer, he was disappointed. He did not need to pretend disappointment was absent in order to remain trusting. He could grieve a hoped-for outcome without declaring the effort meaningless.

Narrator: We were careful not to interpret every delay as a coded sign or every success as proof that a person had discovered a secret spiritual formula. The unseen belongs to Allah, and ordinary events rarely grant us authority to explain His specific wisdom.

Narrator: What faith gave him was a steadier orientation: act lawfully, ask Allah for help, consult knowledgeable people where advice is needed, and resist the urge to make worldly outcomes the measure of one’s worth.
Narrator: This also protected him from blaming others. Another person’s success did not become evidence of superior sincerity, and his own difficulty did not become evidence of divine rejection.
Narrator: Tawhid directs worship, hope, fear, and reliance to Allah alone. It does not invite us to make claims about people’s hearts or to neglect the means Allah has made available.

Narrator: The job search eventually changed shape, but that is not the point of the story. The point is that faithful action can be serious, organised, and patient without pretending to possess the outcome.

title: Why I Stopped Calling Every Coincidence a Sign
script: Narrator: [reflective] For a period, I treated small coincidences as if they carried instructions. A delayed message, a repeated phrase, an unexpected meeting—each seemed to demand interpretation before I could make an ordinary decision.
Narrator: The habit made me anxious rather than wise. I began delaying commitments while waiting for a feeling of certainty that no event could honestly provide.

Narrator: A teacher helped me separate three things: making dua, seeking sound advice, and claiming knowledge of the unseen. The first two are encouraged forms of dependence on Allah; the third is not available to us through private impressions.

Narrator: This did not make life mechanical. It made decisions more responsible. If I needed to choose a course, I considered its purpose, obligations, costs, reliable information, and counsel from people who understood the field.

Narrator: If a matter required a detailed religious ruling, I asked a qualified scholar. If it concerned health, law, or safety, I sought the relevant qualified professional. Spiritual vocabulary was not a substitute for expertise.

Narrator: I also learned that uncertainty is not always a defect to be eliminated. Sometimes the honest response is to make the best lawful decision available and entrust what lies beyond one’s control to Allah.

Narrator: This protected me from another danger: reading misfortune as a verdict about someone’s faith. Difficulty may invite patience and prayer, but it does not authorise spectators to explain another person’s trial.
Narrator: The change was quietly liberating. I still noticed the world with gratitude, but I stopped using ordinary events as a private codebook.
Narrator: Tawhid gave me a clearer centre: worship Allah, use the means that are permitted and appropriate, and leave claims about hidden meanings where they belong—with the One who knows them.

title: How Do We Speak About Trust Without Giving False Promises?
script: Interviewer: [thoughtful] A listener says that encouragement about trust in Allah sometimes sounds like a guarantee that a hardship will end in the way she hopes. How should we speak more carefully?
Analyst: We should distinguish faith from prediction. We can affirm that Allah is wise, merciful, and worthy of reliance without claiming to know the timing or shape of a particular outcome.
Interviewer: What does practical reliance include?

Analyst: It includes prayer, lawful effort, consultation, and using appropriate means. Someone facing a medical concern should seek proper care; someone facing a legal matter should obtain suitable advice.
Interviewer: Why is that distinction important?
Analyst: Because religious language can be misused to pressure people into waiting, silence, or avoidable risk. Trust does not require abandoning responsibility.
Interviewer: Can we say that hardship always has one identifiable lesson?
Analyst: No. We may reflect on broad teachings about patience and dependence on Allah, but we should not announce why a specific person is suffering or what Allah has decreed for them.
Interviewer: How can friends offer support?
Analyst: Ask what is useful, make dua, help with practical tasks where appropriate, and avoid measuring someone’s faith by their emotional response or recovery.
Interviewer: What if a person feels disappointed after making sincere dua?
Analyst: They can bring that pain to Allah honestly. Human grief does not cancel reliance, and no one should be shamed for needing time, support, or qualified help.
Interviewer: What is the balanced message?
Analyst: Rely upon Allah wholeheartedly, take responsible means, and do not turn hope into a promise that a human speaker has no right to make.
Interviewer: What language should we avoid when supporting someone?
Analyst: Avoid saying that a particular event proves Allah is pleased or displeased with them, or that a quick outcome is the measure of sincere reliance.
Interviewer: What language is better?
Analyst: We can say: I am here, I will make dua, and let us consider the responsible next step together.
